summary:
Every fire calendar assumes satellites look at the same hour every year. They don't, and neither do the fires.

FireClock is a free web app that joins 26 years of fire detections from five MODIS and VIIRS satellites into one consistent burning calendar for any area: monthly activity since 2000, this month against the historical normal, critical burning periods, a 90% uncertainty range on every value, and CSV export.

The challenge cites differing "observation schedules". We found they break the record four ways: the 2012 sensor switch, Terra and Aqua's drifting orbits, the end of S-NPP, and fire lit after the ~1:15 pm pass. Over Punjab and Haryana (3.06 million detections), a naive join's fake 6.1x jump becomes 1.06x, with 7.3% error on years the model never saw.

Then we turned the drift into an instrument. Aqua now passes at 3:32 pm and sees 5.4x more rice-season fire than the ~1:15 pm satellites. A placebo season stays flat, and so does Argentina, where the same code corrects the record too.

Why it matters: these counts judge North India's crop-burning policy. October 2026 read 91% below normal. FireClock shows whether that means fewer fires, or fires the satellites missed.
details:
Website: https://fireclock-team.github.io/fireclock/ · Explorer app: https://fireclock-team.github.io/fireclock/app.html · Technical paper: https://fireclock-team.github.io/fireclock/FireClock_paper.pdf

At a glance: 26 years · 5 satellites · 2 continents · 3.34 million NASA detections · 6 independent checks · 1 new finding.

What it does:

FireClock turns NASA's split fire record (MODIS from 2000, VIIRS from 2012) into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area. Choose a preset, type coordinates or draw a box on the map, and get:

• a month-by-year calendar from 2000 to today on one scale, with a raw/harmonized toggle that shows the fake 2012 jump disappear, and a year-range filter

• the latest month against the 2003–2022 normal, plus the area's critical burning period

• a yearly record with a 90% uncertainty range on every value

• a satellite-clock panel: when each satellite actually looked at this area, year by year, and a warning when counts may be hiding fire

• live analysis for any box: how the burning season has shifted between decades, the months that broke furthest from normal, and the exchange rates behind the conversion

• one-click CSV export

It runs in any browser with no install, login or server. An overview website explains the project with an interactive "satellite clock" you can play through year by year, and the explorer has a 60-second tour for judges.

The problem: four breaks, not one:

The challenge notes that MODIS and VIIRS differ in "observation schedules." We found this breaks the record four ways, and typical harmonization fixes only the first:

1. 2012, new sensor: VIIRS sees far more fire, so a naive join jumps 6.1x.

2. 2020 onward, drifting orbits: Terra and Aqua no longer hold their orbits, so the same MODIS sensor now looks at a different hour every year.

3. 2 November 2026, S-NPP ends: the usual VIIRS reference satellite is gone.

4. Every season, fire after the pass: fire lit after ~1:15 pm is invisible to the satellites most counts rely on.

FireClock handles all four.

How it works:

1. Data pipeline: ~3,900 scripted NASA FIRMS API requests, with quota-aware throttling, caching and automatic resume, collect every MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m detection over both regions. Non-fire hotspots that NASA labels (factories, gas flares, volcanoes) are removed: 37,781 in India, 89,623 in Argentina.

2. Measuring the clock: every detection's timestamp is converted to local solar time, so each satellite's real look time is measured per area, season and year instead of assumed from orbit tables.

3. One VIIRS scale: NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are bridged to S-NPP (x0.96, x0.99) and averaged, never added, so more satellites never means more fire and the record continues past S-NPP's end.

4. Pre-drift calibration: the MODIS→VIIRS exchange rate is learned for each calendar month using only 2013–2020, before the drift. It ranges from 1.6 (August) to 10.7 (June), so one fixed factor would distort the seasons. Aqua's rate moved from 6.4 to 4.8 by 2026, an error that calibrating on all overlap years would absorb. Monthly rates are shrunk toward the annual rate, with the strength tuned by leave-one-year-out cross-validation. A Terra-only bridge covers 2000–2002.

5. Uncertainty: a 500x year-block bootstrap plus Poisson counting noise gives a 90% range for every month.

6. App: monthly totals stored on a 0.25° grid; the browser sums any drawn box and runs every analysis instantly, so the whole tool is a static site.

Results (Punjab & Haryana, 3,057,777 detections):

• Fake 2012 jump: 6.1x → 1.06x.

• Validation on years the model never saw (each of 2013–2020 held out, then predicted): 7.3% median annual error, R² 0.983 (Aqua 6.0%, Terra 10.7%).

• The finding: as Aqua's look time drifted, it saw x1.33 (2023, 1:37 pm) → x1.60 (2024, 2:05 pm) → x2.26 (2025, 2:43 pm) → x5.44 (2026, 3:32 pm) as much rice-season fire as the fixed ~1:15 pm VIIRS satellites.

• The season itself has moved: the peak burning month shifted from October (2003–2012) to November (2017–2026).

Six checks that it's real:

1. Placebo: same satellite, same drift, wheat season stays flat (x0.6–1.3).

2. Dose-response: the effect grows every year as the look time moves later.

3. Same-day test: two identical VIIRS instruments, same fields, same day, up to an hour apart: +29% fire per hour later (90% CI 25–34%, 680 days; pair fixed effects, bootstrap CI).

4. Viewing angle: pixel size controlled as a covariate.

5. Independent evidence: matches a 2026 geostationary-satellite study of the region.

6. Second continent: over Argentina, Aqua at 3:55 pm sees x1.1, so there is no satellite artifact. The x5.4 reflects when Punjab burns.

Same code, another continent (Paraná Delta, Argentina, 280,737 detections):

Run with zero changes. The naive join calls 2020 the Delta's worst fire year (80,075 detections); FireClock shows 2008 was bigger (61,902, 90% range 48,848–73,718), the year Delta smoke blanketed Buenos Aires. The fake 2012 jump drops from 3.6x to 0.68x, matching MODIS alone (0.75x). Validation there is weaker (12.3% error, R² 0.86) because fires are fewer and burstier, and we report it as is.

How is it creative?

Orbit drift is normally a nuisance to correct. We turned it into an instrument: Aqua sliding across the afternoon became a slow scan that measures fire the fixed satellites can't see, a natural experiment run on NASA's own orbit change. And rather than assume when satellites look, FireClock measures it from the data.

Benefits and intended impact:

Every autumn, crop-residue smoke from Punjab and Haryana adds to some of the worst air on Earth, and satellite fire counts are how that burning, and the policies against it, are judged. The harmonized October 2026 count is 91% below normal. If counts depend on what time the satellite looks, a falling trend can be mistaken for success. FireClock gives fire managers, air-quality agencies, scientists and journalists a 26-year record on one scale, uncertainty on every month, and a warning when the satellite clock may be hiding fire. With S-NPP gone and Terra and Aqua near their end, this is what keeps the fire record usable.

What factors did we consider?

• Validity: calibrate only on pre-drift years, test on years the model never saw, and require a placebo and a second region before trusting any finding.

• Honest limits: our same-day effect is similar before and after 2022, so we don't claim to date a shift in burning time (the cited geostationary study reports one). A hotspot is a detection, not a burned area. The 2026 season runs to 13 November.

• Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palette, plain-language labels, reduced-motion support, works on phones, no install or account.

• Openness and reproducibility: MIT licence; one command per step rebuilds everything from NASA FIRMS; a 29-page technical paper documents every equation, table and check.

Tools, languages and software:

Python (pandas, NumPy, Requests, Matplotlib) for the pipeline, statistics and figures; HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the website and explorer; LaTeX for the paper; GitHub Pages for hosting.

Use of AI: FireClock was built with AI-assisted development (Claude, Anthropic) for coding, framing and drafting. The author chose the scientific question and approach, ran the NASA data pipeline, made the analysis decisions, and checked every result. All figures are computed directly from NASA FIRMS data by the open-source code, and no AI-generated images, audio, or video are used. AI-generated images mention the same below in the slides.
